title: WHY DID LEVITICUS FORBID SEX DURING MENSTRUATION?
paragraphs:
WHY DID LEVITICUS FORBID SEX DURING MENSTRUATION?
The Command Almost Everyone Misunderstands—and What It Reveals About Holiness, Intimacy, Blood, and the Grace of Jesus Christ
There are verses in the Bible people underline.
There are verses people frame.
There are verses people quote when they are afraid, grieving, confused, or desperately trying to hold onto faith.
And then there are verses people quietly hurry past.
Leviticus 18:19 is one of them.
It speaks about menstruation.
It speaks about sex.
It speaks about something so private that many Christians have probably never heard a sermon about it.
And yet God put it in Scripture.
That alone should make us stop.
Because if we believe that “all Scripture is breathed out by God” (2 Timothy 3:16), then we cannot treat uncomfortable passages as embarrassing leftovers from an ancient religion.
We have to ask the uncomfortable question.
Why?
Why would the God who created marriage, sexuality, the female body, fertility, blood, desire, and intimacy tell Israel that sexual intercourse was forbidden during menstruation?
Was menstruation sinful?
Was God shaming women?
Was this merely an ancient health regulation?
Does the command apply directly to Christians today?
And perhaps the question underneath all those questions is this:
What does any of this have to do with Jesus?
Stay with this until the end.
Because what begins with a command concerning blood eventually forces us to confront something much closer to home:
the difference between being physically unclean under Israel's covenant and being morally guilty before a holy God...
and the breathtaking reason Christians can never read Leviticus correctly without eventually looking toward Christ.
The Hebrew of Leviticus 18:19 says:
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve’el-ishshah beniddat tum’atah lo tiqrav legalot ervatah.
A careful rendering is:
“You shall not approach a woman in her menstrual impurity to uncover her nakedness.”
Three expressions deserve attention.
נִדָּה — niddah
The word is associated here with menstruation and the condition of menstrual impurity.
טֻמְאָה — tum’ah
This means impurity or uncleanness.
And then:
לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ — legalot ervatah
Literally, “to uncover her nakedness,” an expression used in the sexual laws of Leviticus.
So we should begin by refusing to soften what the passage actually says.
Leviticus 18:19 prohibits sexual relations during menstrual impurity.
Leviticus 20:18 makes the prohibition even more explicit:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה דָּוָה וְגִלָּה אֶת־עֶרְוָתָהּ אֶת־מְקֹרָהּ הֶעֱרָה וְהִיא גִּלְּתָה אֶת־מְקוֹר דָּמֶיהָ וְנִכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּם׃
The text describes a man lying sexually with a menstruating woman, exposing the source of her blood, and declares that both are to be “cut off” from among their people.
This was not presented to Israel as optional advice.
But now we have to notice something that changes the conversation.
Menstruation itself was not a moral sin.
That distinction matters enormously.

Leviticus 15 places menstruation inside a much larger system of ritual purity and impurity. Male bodily discharges appear there too. Sexual emission could result in temporary uncleanness. Childbirth also involved ritual impurity elsewhere in Leviticus.
None of those realities means that the body itself was evil.
None means that being female was sinful.
None means that a menstruating woman had committed some moral offense simply because her body was functioning normally.
This is where careless teaching can wound people.
Biblical “uncleanness” is not automatically identical with personal moral guilt.
A person could become ritually unclean without committing a sin.
That distinction is essential for understanding Leviticus.
God was teaching Israel to live within categories of holy and common, clean and unclean, permitted and forbidden.
Israel was not merely another ancient nation with a religious decoration attached to its culture.
They belonged to Yahweh.
Their worship belonged to Him.
Their food belonged under His authority.
Their calendar belonged under His authority.
Their bodies belonged under His authority.
And yes...
their sexuality belonged under His authority too.
That may be one of the most confronting lessons in the entire passage.
Because modern culture often treats sexual desire as virtually sovereign.
“If I desire it, why should anyone tell me no?”
“If two people want it, what business does God have interfering?”
But Scripture begins somewhere radically different.
The body belongs to its Creator.
Sex is not outside God's jurisdiction.
Marriage is not outside God's jurisdiction.
Desire is not outside God's jurisdiction.
Even the most private room in the house is not a place where God suddenly stops being Lord.
And perhaps that is where this ancient command begins reaching into our modern lives.
Not because every ritual boundary given to Israel is automatically a command imposed unchanged upon the church...
but because the God revealed in Scripture has never surrendered His authority over human sexuality.
There is another important detail.
Blood occupies an extraordinary place in Leviticus.
Later, Leviticus 17:11 declares:
כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הַבָּשָׂר בַּדָּם הִוא
Ki nefesh habbasar badam hi.
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood.”
But we need to be careful here.
It is tempting to build an elaborate explanation and say, “Therefore this is exactly why intercourse during menstruation was prohibited.”
The Bible itself does not explicitly give that explanation in Leviticus 18:19.
So we should not pretend God said something He did not say.
Various explanations have been proposed across Jewish and Christian history—ritual, theological, symbolic, social, and even medical.
Some may contain useful observations.
But faithful interpretation requires humility.
We can confidently say what God commanded.
We can understand that command within Leviticus' larger concern for holiness, purity, blood, sexuality, and Israel's covenant identity.
But where Scripture does not explicitly say, “This is the sole reason why,” we should resist turning an inference into revelation.
Sometimes reverence means refusing to make the Bible say more than it says.
And this is where another question becomes unavoidable.
What does this mean for Christians?
This is where Jesus must become central rather than being attached to the end of the discussion as a religious afterthought.
Christians do not approach Leviticus as though Jesus never came.
The New Testament presents Jesus as the fulfillment toward which the law and sacrificial system point.
Jesus said:
“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets... I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17).
Hebrews tells us that the old covenant contained shadows pointing toward realities fulfilled in Christ.
And something remarkable happens when Jesus enters the world of ritual impurity.
He touches people others feared touching.
A leper comes to Him.
Jesus touches him.
A woman suffering from a flow of blood for twelve years reaches through a crowd and touches His garment.
Think about that scene.
Twelve years.
Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years of suffering.
Twelve years of doctors.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Mark tells us she “had suffered much under many physicians” and had spent everything she possessed, yet instead of improving she became worse.
Then she heard about Jesus.
She pushed through the crowd.
Perhaps terrified.
Perhaps ashamed.
Perhaps desperate enough that embarrassment no longer mattered.
And she touched His garment.
Immediately, the bleeding stopped.
Jesus turned.
“Who touched my garments?”
The disciples were confused because everyone was pressing against Him.
But Jesus knew.
The woman came trembling.
She fell before Him.
And told Him the whole truth.
Imagine how exposed she must have felt.
Then Jesus called her something beautiful.
“Daughter.”
Not contamination.
Not embarrassment.
Not inconvenience.
Daughter.
“Your faith has made you well; go in peace.”
That is Jesus.
Under ordinary purity logic, uncleanness spreads through contact.
But when the unclean encounter Christ, something astonishing happens.
His holiness is not defeated by their uncleanness.
His purity overwhelms what defiles.
The sick encounter Him and healing flows outward.
The rejected encounter Him and dignity returns.
The guilty encounter Him and discover mercy.
The spiritually dead encounter Him and life walks out of the tomb.

And suddenly Leviticus begins sounding less like an irrelevant collection of strange ancient restrictions and more like the vocabulary of a world desperately waiting for Someone holy enough to deal with uncleanness once and for all.
But there is an even deeper problem than ritual impurity.
Sin.
Because you and I may never have violated Leviticus 18:19...
and still desperately need a Savior.
Maybe your uncleanness has nothing to do with menstrual blood.
Maybe it is hidden in your browser history.
Maybe it is the message thread you keep deleting.
Maybe it is the affair nobody discovered.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is bitterness.
Maybe it is pride disguised as spirituality.
Maybe it is envy that smiles in public.
Maybe you know exactly how to raise your hands during worship while refusing to surrender the one room in your heart you have locked against God.
Maybe everyone thinks you are spiritually strong.
But you know.
You know what happens when nobody is watching.
You know what thought keeps returning.
You know what relationship crossed a boundary.
You know what compromise you renamed so you would not have to call it sin.
You know what God has been asking you to surrender.
And perhaps this is why Leviticus makes us uncomfortable.
Because holiness always becomes uncomfortable when we have grown comfortable with compromise.
We want a Jesus who comforts us.
Scripture gives us that Jesus.
But Scripture also gives us the Jesus who says:
“Repent.”
We want grace.
Thank God, grace is real.
But biblical grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin at unimaginable cost to Himself.
The cross is where nobody can honestly say sin is trivial.
Look at Jesus.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
Bleeding.
And there is the scandal at the center of Christianity:
the Holy One taking the place of the guilty.
Peter writes:
Paul says:
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
The blood imagery that runs through Scripture reaches its climactic Christian meaning not in menstruation, but in the sacrificial death of Christ.
Hebrews declares:
“Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.”
And then it points beyond repeated sacrifices toward Jesus.
Christ does what bulls and goats could never finally accomplish.
He offers Himself.
Once for all.
That changes how Christians read passages about purity.
We do not mock them.
We do not erase them.
We do not pretend they were meaningless.
We read them through the fulfillment accomplished by Jesus Christ.

The Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 did not place the entire Mosaic ritual system upon Gentile believers. Paul likewise warns against treating old-covenant calendar and food regulations as the basis of justification before God.
Christians therefore need wisdom when moving from an old-covenant command to new-covenant practice.
We should neither casually impose every Israelite purity regulation unchanged upon Christians nor throw Leviticus away as though holiness no longer matters.
The covenantal administration has changed.
The holiness of God has not.
And maybe that is the word somebody reading this desperately needs.
Grace did not make holiness irrelevant.
Grace made holiness possible in people who could never make themselves clean.
Jesus did not die so that we could become comfortable with the sins destroying us.
He died to save us from them.
Maybe you have spent years hiding.
Maybe your secret has become so familiar that you no longer remember who you were before it.
Maybe shame has convinced you that if people knew everything about you, they would leave.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
Every chapter.
Every deleted message.
Every night.
Every compromise.
Every relapse.
Every rationalization.
Every wound beneath the behavior.
He knows what happened to you.
And He knows what you chose afterward.
Yet the Gospel invitation still stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to approach Christ.
You approach Christ because you cannot clean yourself.
That bleeding woman did not wait until she was healed before reaching for Jesus.
She reached because she needed healing.
And maybe spiritually, that is you.
Still bleeding somewhere nobody sees.
Still smiling.
Still working.
Still posting.
Still going to church.
Still telling people, “I'm okay.”
But exhausted.
Jesus is not asking you to become impressive.
He is calling you to come into the light.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Let other believers see it.
Let somebody pray.
Let somebody realize they are not fighting alone.
And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become another person's reason not to give up tonight.
Because the Gospel is not the story of good people proving how clean they are.
It is the story of sinners discovering that Jesus Christ can do what they could never do for themselves.
From impurity...
to cleansing.
From guilt...
to forgiveness.
From bondage...
to freedom.
From hiding...
to confession.
From death...
to life.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this article helped you see a difficult passage of Scripture differently, don't let it disappear into your feed.
There will be a day when someone asks you why Christians still bother reading Leviticus.
Come back to this.
Study the passages yourself.
Test what you read against Scripture.
Not as a performance.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
God's grace cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid that price.
Open your Bible.
Look at Leviticus again.
Then keep reading until you reach Matthew.
Keep reading until the woman with the flow of blood touches Jesus.
Keep reading until Jesus carries the cross.
Keep reading until blood runs from the body of the spotless Lamb.
Keep reading until the stone is rolled away.
Keep reading until you understand:
The Bible's story was never about humanity climbing high enough to reach a holy God.
It is about the Holy God coming down to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
So share the truth.
Save what strengthens your faith.
And then do not leave it as a comment.
Take it to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His mercy.
Walk differently.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that you are unclean.
The greatest tragedy would be standing within reach of the One who cleanses sinners...
and choosing to keep hiding.
The hands you are afraid to approach are the very hands that were pierced to bring you home.
